citation: Statement on the first bridges over the branches of the Chicago River, agreed at a meeting of old settlers held late in the fall of 1883 and signed J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble; presented to the editors by John Bates and printed as a footnote in Andreas, History of Chicago, vol. 1 (Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884), pp. 631-632.
author: J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver, John Noble
repository: Printed in Andreas 1884 vol. 1; no separate manuscript located.
locator: vol. 1, footnote running across pp. 631-632, in the 'Wolf Point and Early Hotels' chapter
note: THE ONLY DESCRIPTION ANYBODY WROTE OF HOW THE BRANCH BRIDGES WERE PUT TOGETHER, and four men who used them signed it. Andreas prints it as a footnote to his own narrative, which is why it has been read past for so long: the paragraph above it is the famous 'formed of stringers and only fitted for foot passengers', and the evidence that contradicts the picture that sentence paints is set in six-point type at the foot of the facing page. Read as printed: 'both bridges were built on abutments and two "bents." The abutments were built of logs in the shallow water near the banks. The bents were of four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water. Stringers of heavy logs stretched from the abutments to the bents, and between the bents. On these stringers puncheons or split logs were laid for a floor. These bridges were about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years, after which guards, or railings, were added. These were both wagon bridges, and were about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice freely.' The North Branch sentence that follows is Cleaver's: 'Cleaver remembers driving across the first bridge over the North Branch; it was a wagon bridge, ten or twelve feet wide.' TIER 2 AND NOT TIER 1: it is a recollection set down fifty-one years after the structure was built, by men recalling their own use of it. Its authority is that four of them agreed, in writing, over their signatures, and that what they describe is joinery rather than dates. WHY IT IS TRUSTED ON THE MIDDLE OF THE BRIDGE AND NOT ON WHEN IT WAS BUILT: the bents, the stringers, the puncheon floor and the six-foot clearance are the kind of thing a man who drove a team over a structure knows; the letter's build date (winter of 1831-32) is the same date Cleaver gave the Tribune in 1893 and disagrees with Andreas's own prose, so the disagreement stands where it stood. Two independent scans of the volume were read against each other because the OCR of the footnote is poor in both: archive.org items historyofchicago01andr and historyofchicago01inandr. Every sentence quoted above is one the two readings agree on; the South Branch dates in the same footnote are NOT, and are therefore not cited anywhere in this dataset.
access_notes: 1883 statement printed in an 1884 volume; public domain. The footnote sits at the foot of pp. 631-632 and is easy to miss in the full-text index — search for 'bents' or 'puncheons' rather than for bridge. The second scan (historyofchicago01inandr) has the cleaner OCR of the two.
